title: Language core: OOP, equality and hashing (Python)
seriesDescription: ABCs, Protocols, dataclasses, composition, __eq__ and __hash__. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: ABC and Protocol, dataclasses, MRO and super(), composition over inheritance, class vs instance attributes, and the __eq__/__hash__ contract with its mutable-key traps.
source: Python docs: abc, dataclasses, data model (__eq__, __hash__), typing.Protocol, the C3 method resolution order; Real Python; Fluent Python (Ramalho); Toptal and GeeksforGeeks Python interview lists

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about Python abstract base classes.
questions.text: A class that inherits from abc.ABC and leaves a method decorated with @{1} unimplemented raises {2} as soon as you try to instantiate it.
questions.explanation: The check happens at instantiation, not at class definition. `NotImplementedError` is what a plain base-class method raises by convention when you do not use `ABC`.

questions.prompt: Match each Python construct to what it is for.

right.text: Structural typing: any class with matching methods satisfies it for the type checker
Nominal base class: a subclass that skips an abstract method cannot be instantiated
Generates `__init__`, `__eq__` and `__hash__` and blocks attribute assignment
Removes the per-instance `__dict__`, saving memory and rejecting new attributes
Tuple subclass with named fields: immutable and unpackable

questions.explanation: Protocol is for structural typing, ABC for enforced contracts, frozen dataclass for hashable value objects, `__slots__` for compact instances.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Inheritance couples a subclass to its superclass more tightly than composition couples a wrapper to a collaborator.
questions.reason: A subclass can depend on implementation details of the superclass, such as which overridable methods call each other.

whys.a: Correct: the fragile base class problem is exactly this hidden dependence, which a wrapper that only uses the public API avoids.
whys.b: R is not merely true, it is the reason A holds.
whys.c: R is true: self-use of overridable methods is a documented source of bugs.
whys.d: A is true; The classic design guideline says to favour composition over inheritance.

questions.explanation: Design for inheritance or prohibit it. Composition plus delegation (forwarding class) keeps the dependency to the public contract.

questions.prompt: Write a Python frozen dataclass named `Point` with `float` fields `x` and `y` so that instances are immutable and hashable.
questions.explanation: `frozen=True` makes assignment raise `FrozenInstanceError` and, together with the default `eq=True`, generates `__hash__` from the fields. A `NamedTuple` would also work but is not what the question asks.

questions.prompt: A class must explicitly inherit from a `typing.Protocol` to satisfy it for a static type checker such as `mypy`.

options.why: Protocols are structural: the base class is not required.
Correct: `mypy` checks the method signatures, so no inheritance is needed (only `@runtime_checkable` matters for `isinstance`).

questions.explanation: That is the difference between nominal (ABC) and structural (Protocol) typing, the Python counterpart of Go-style interfaces.

questions.prompt: In Python 3, a class that defines `__eq__` but does not define `__hash__` gets its `__hash__` set to `None`, so its instances cannot be put in a set or used as dict keys.

options.why: Correct: defining `__eq__` implicitly sets `__hash__ = None`, which is why `{P(1)}` raises `TypeError`.
Wrong: Python 3 does not keep the inherited identity hash once `__eq__` is overridden, because equal objects must hash equally.

questions.explanation: Python refuses to guess a hash consistent with your new equality. Add `__hash__` over the same immutable fields, or use `@dataclass(frozen=True)`. Verified by running it: set literal raises `TypeError: unhashable type`.

options.text: `BCA, following the C3 order D, B, C, A`
options.why: Correct: the `C3` `MRO` of D is D, B, C, A and `super()` follows it, so B calls C, which calls A.

options.text: `BA, since super() goes to the declared parent`
options.why: Wrong: `super()` in B does not jump straight to its declared parent A; it goes to the next class in the instance `MRO`, which is C.

options.text: `BAC, since C runs after A finishes`
options.why: Wrong: A is the common base, so `C3` linearisation places it after both B and C, never between them.
Wrong: B and C list A consistently, so a valid linearisation exists and the class statement succeeds.

questions.explanation: Python uses `C3` linearisation (`D.__mro__`). Cooperative `super()` visits every class once in that order; this ordering removes the classic diamond ambiguity for classes.

questions.prompt:
A subclass of `dict` increments `self.count` inside `__setitem__` before calling `super().__setitem__`. Then:

```python
d = CountingDict()
d.update({"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3})
d["d"] = 4
```

What is `d.count` at the end?
questions.explanation: CPython's `dict.update` does not call an overridden `__setitem__`, so only the final assignment is counted. Subclassing built-ins relies on implementation details; composition (wrap a `dict` and forward) avoids the trap.

questions.prompt:
Consider

```python
x = [1, 2]
y = x
z = [1, 2]
```

How many of these four expressions are True: `x is y`, `x == z`, `x is z`, `x is not z`?
questions.explanation: `x is y` is True (same object), `x == z` is True (equal values), `x is z` is False (different objects), `x is not z` is True. `==` compares values via `__eq__`, is compares identity.

questions.prompt: Write a Python class `Point` with `x` and `y` whose instances are equal when `x` and `y` match and can be used as dict keys (define `__eq__` and `__hash__`).
questions.explanation: Objects that compare equal must hash equal; hash the same fields that `__eq__` compares. A frozen dataclass does all of this for you.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code do?

```python
cache = {}
key = [1, 2]
cache[key] = "v"
print(len(cache))
```

What is the outcome?

options.why: Correct: lists are mutable and define `__eq__` without a stable hash, so they cannot be dict keys.

options.text: `It prints 1 because the list is stored as a key`
options.why: The assignment fails before anything is stored.

options.text: `It prints 0 because lists are ignored as keys`
options.why: Python never silently ignores a key; it raises instead.
`KeyError` is raised by a failed lookup, not by storing a key.

questions.explanation: Use a `tuple` (immutable, hashable if its items are) when a sequence must be a key.

questions.prompt: Select all that can be used as `dict` keys.

options.why: Strings are immutable and hashable.
A `tuple` is hashable when all its items are.
`frozenset` is the immutable, hashable set.
Lists are mutable and unhashable.
Dicts are mutable and unhashable.
Hashing a `tuple` hashes its items, so the inner `list` makes it unhashable.

questions.explanation: Hashable means a stable hash for the object lifetime and a consistent `__eq__`; built-in immutable types qualify, containers only if everything inside does.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

```python
class Cart:
    items = []

a = Cart()
b = Cart()
a.items.append("x")
print(b.items)
```

What is the output?

options.text: `['x'], because one list lives on the class and all instances share it`
options.why: Correct: `items` is one list stored on the class and shared by every instance.

options.text: `[], because b never appended anything to its own list`
options.why: It would be empty only if each instance had its own list created in `__init__`.
Lookup falls back from the instance to the class attribute.
Class attributes can be mutated freely; the list is an ordinary object.

questions.explanation: Create per-instance mutable state in `__init__` (`self.items = []`), not as a class attribute.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Instances of a plain Python class are hashable by default.
questions.reason: Python derives the default hash from the values of all the instance attributes.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: A is true, but the default hash comes from the object identity, so R is false.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: A is true, but the default hash comes from the object identity, so R is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true, but the default hash comes from the object identity, so R is false.
whys.d: This option says A is false and R is true, which does not match: A is true, but the default hash comes from the object identity, so R is false.

questions.explanation: The default `__eq__` and `__hash__` are identity-based. Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__` sets `__hash__` to `None`.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A dataclass declared with `@dataclass(frozen=True)` can be used as a dict key.
questions.reason: Assigning to an attribute of a frozen dataclass instance raises `FrozenInstanceError`.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: Both statements are true, but hashability comes from eq=True plus frozen=True generating __hash__, not from the error on assignment.
whys.b: Correct: Both statements are true, but hashability comes from eq=True plus frozen=True generating __hash__, not from the error on assignment.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: Both statements are true, but hashability comes from eq=True plus frozen=True generating __hash__, not from the error on assignment.
whys.d: This option says A is false and R is true, which does not match: Both statements are true, but hashability comes from eq=True plus frozen=True generating __hash__, not from the error on assignment.

questions.explanation: Frozen plus eq makes the dataclass generate `__hash__` from its fields.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Python dataclass declared with `@dataclass(frozen=True)` is unhashable.
questions.reason: A dataclass with `eq=True` and `frozen=False` gets `__hash__` set to `None`.

whys.a: A is false, so this cannot be right.
whys.c: R is true, so option c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: frozen=True with eq=True generates __hash__ from the fields, so A is false; R is true (the default mutable dataclass is unhashable).

questions.explanation: `eq=True`, `frozen=False` sets `__hash__` to `None`; `eq=True`, `frozen=True` generates a field-based `__hash__`; `unsafe_hash=True` forces one.
